title: Dynamic slot reclaimer and smooth evictor adapter for fragmentation mitigation
author: Eleanor Park
description:
Motivation: Production clusters observed increased KV cache fragmentation under mixed-length sessions, causing frequent small-page spills and uneven memory pressure between tenants. This PR introduces a runtime-side fragmentation sensor and a graded (smooth) eviction adapter that cooperates with the scheduler and continuous-batching layer to reduce tail latency and spill frequency.

What changed (high level): added a low-cost fragmentation sensor that tracks free-slot distribution and local occupancy variance per arena; implemented a dynamic slot reclaimer that opportunistically coalesces adjacent free slots without global stops-the-world compactions; introduced a graded eviction adapter that smooths eviction aggressiveness based on sensor signals and tenant pressure; added anticipatory paging hints so the kernel-selection layer can prefer compact-friendly layouts during hot sequences; exposed metrics and tracing to the console for visibility.

Checklist: [x] unit tests for sensor heuristics, [x] e2e perf harness against perf-canary workload, [x] migration path for existing allocator configs, [x] docs draft for console and ops runbook, [x] feature-flag gating for staged rollout.

Commit summary (single-string list below):
- Add fragmentation sensor (runtime/kv/frag_sensor.rs) and related metrics
- Implement DynamicSlotReclaimer with gentle coalescing pass (runtime/kv/reclaimer.go)
- GradedEvictorAdapter: translate sensor signals to eviction windows (runtime/kv/evictor_adapter.cc)
- Hook anticipatory paging hints into kernel selector (runtime/compilation/kernels.go)
- Integrate with continuous-batching to avoid batch amplification during reclaim passes (runtime/batching/controller.py)
- Tests, benchmarks, documentation and feature-flag gating

Files/areas changed (high level): runtime/kv/{frag_sensor.rs,reclaimer.go,evictor_adapter.cc}, runtime/compilation/kernels.go, runtime/batching/controller.py, observability/metrics/kv_frag_metrics.yaml, docs/ops/kv-reclamation.md, tests/perf/cluster_fragmentation_test.sh. No API surface changes to user-facing inference API.

Benchmarks: On the perf-canary mixed-length session trace (p99 tokens per second workload) we saw: 12% reduction in p99 latency for generation endpoints, 18% fewer spill-to-disk events under sustained 85% resident memory, and a 7% improvement in end-to-end token throughput due to reduced fragmentation-induced requeuing. Microbenchmarks show the sensor adds <0.8% CPU at steady state.

Rollout plan: gated behind feature flag kv.gradedEvictor. Canary rollout to two Dedicated regions for 3 days, monitor kv_frag_score, spill_rate, batch_latency. If regressions discovered, auto-fallback to previous evictor policy (built into adapter).

Migration notes: configuration knobs preserved; new knobs documented under docs/ops/kv-reclamation.md. No tenant data migration required.

Related work: follows up on ENG-2145 (observation telemetry) and complements ENG-2210 (batching-scheduler co-op).

review_comments: Derek Huang (review): Can you quantify reclaimer CPU tax and show behavior under extreme churn? Also, prefer a more deterministic coalesce pass to avoid fairness issues.
Eleanor Park (reply): Added microbenchmarks showing <0.8% CPU and updated algorithm to bound coalesce budget per epoch. See reclaimer.go comments and tests.
Nina Patel (review): The adapter contract with the scheduler needs clearer invariants for batch safety — if reclaim triggers in the middle of a large batch we see token reordering in local tests.

Eleanor Park (reply): Hooked into batching controller to delay aggressive reclaim until current batch commit; added e2e test to prevent reordering. Also added metrics for batch-delay induced by reclaiming.
Owen McCarthy (approval): Verified perf runs and canary simulation. Approving with the feature flag and runbook additions.
